**MTH 341 — Week 4: Determinants of Matrix Sums**

Due: 2026-10-23
Due time: 11:59 p.m. PDT
Date imported: 2026-10-23
Source: [Canvas](https://canvas.oregonstate.edu/groups/750466/discussion_topics/11698213)
Response source: Jacob Peterson, entry 43183864, posted 2026-10-23 at 11:16 p.m.

Your original response is preserved in the answer reveal, with equations transcribed into LaTeX. The verification feedback is an independently authored addition.

## Instructions

Determine whether the proposed determinant identity is true. Prove it if true; otherwise give a counterexample and identify the matrix sizes for which it holds as an identity.
content.title: Assignment information

correctAnswer.value:
**Your original response — Jacob Peterson (entry 43183864)**

The statement is false for matrices larger than 1x1. Given:

$$A = B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$$

Adding the matrices and calculating the determinants gives:

$$\det(A+B)=\begin{vmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{vmatrix}=4$$

$$\det(A)+\det(B)=1+1=2$$

Since 4 does not equal 2, the statement is false.

However, it is true for 1x1 matrices because the determinant is just the single entry.

$$A=[a],\quad B=[b]$$

$$\det(A+B)=a+b=\det(A)+\det(B)$$

Therefore, the statement is always true for 1x1 matrices, but not for matrices 2x2 or larger.

content.problem:
Source question: Canvas topic 11698213, Question 1. Only this mathematical question and your response to it are included.

Determine whether

$$\det(A+B)=\det(A)+\det(B).$$

If it is true, prove it. Otherwise, give a counterexample. If it is false in general, for what size matrices is the statement true?

Here $A$ and $B$ are square matrices of the same size.

Your response: {{response}}
content.solution:
**Authored verification.** Your $2\times2$ counterexample is correct: $A=B=I_2$ gives $A+B=2I_2$, whose determinant is $2\cdot2-0\cdot0=4$, while $\det(A)+\det(B)=1+1=2$. Your argument for $1\times1$ matrices also proves the identity for every pair of that size.

To justify the conclusion for every larger size, take $A=B=I_n$. Then

$$\det(A+B)=\det(2I_n)=2^n,\qquad \det(A)+\det(B)=2.$$

For every integer $n\ge2$, $2^n>2$. Thus, among positive matrix sizes, $1\times1$ is the only size for which the equality holds for **all** pairs. It can still hold for particular larger pairs, for example when $B=0$; the conclusion concerns a universal identity.

The determinant is linear in one row at a time when all other rows are fixed. That property does not imply additivity when an entire matrix is added.

content.solution: The **trivial solution** sets every unknown equal to zero. A homogeneous system has the form $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$, and $A\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$, so this solution always exists. If the solution is unique, it must be this zero solution. The name applies to the zero solution even when other solutions also exist.

correctAnswer.value:
The span is every vector I can reach by scaling the given vectors and adding them together, allowing any real coefficients. In symbols,

$$\operatorname{span}\{\vec v_1,\ldots,\vec v_k\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_i\vec v_i:c_1,\ldots,c_k\in\mathbb R\right\}.$$

Geometrically, one nonzero vector spans a line through the origin. Two nonparallel vectors span a plane through the origin. Three linearly independent vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ span all of $\mathbb R^3$. A set consisting only of the zero vector spans just the origin.

content.problem:
Source question: Canvas Question 2 (question_59459087).

**Reading definition** (unnumbered source item question_59459086, immediately before Question 2): Let $\vec v_1,\ldots,\vec v_k$ and $\vec u$ be column vectors. The vector $\vec u$ is a **linear combination** of $\{\vec v_1,\ldots,\vec v_k\}$ if scalars $c_1,\ldots,c_k$ exist such that

$$
\vec u=\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_i\vec v_i.
$$

Write in your own words what the span of a set of vectors is. Is there a geometric way that you think about spans?

Your response: {{answer}}
content.solution: A span contains **all** linear combinations, rather than just the original vectors or one particular sum. The coefficients may be positive, negative, or zero, so a single nonzero vector gives the entire line through the origin, rather than only a ray or segment. With more vectors, the geometric size depends on how many independent directions they supply, rather than just how many vectors are listed.

content.problem:
Source question: Canvas Question 3 (question_59459088). The source's follow-up refers to the first paragraph on page 194 of the assigned reading.

Is the zero vector in the span of a set of nonzero vectors?
content.solution:
Set $c_1=\cdots=c_k=0$. Then

$$0\vec v_1+\cdots+0\vec v_k=\vec0,$$

which shows directly that the zero vector belongs to the span. This works for independent and dependent sets alike. Merely obtaining zero does not prove dependence: dependence requires a combination with **at least one nonzero coefficient**. This also explains the source's follow-up asking why; its reading reference is the first paragraph on page 194.

topicCoverage.title: Linear Span of Vectors in N-Dimensional Euclidean Space

correctAnswer.value:
The vectors are linearly independent when none can be built as a linear combination of the others. Each vector contributes a direction outside the span of the others. Equivalently,

$$c_1\vec v_1+\cdots+c_k\vec v_k=\vec0$$

forces $c_1=\cdots=c_k=0$.

Geometrically, two nonzero vectors are independent when they are not parallel. In $\mathbb R^3$, three independent vectors do not all lie in a plane through the origin, so together they span three-dimensional space.

content.solution: The test concerns linear combinations of **all** vectors in the set. For two vectors, being nonparallel is sufficient. For three or more, checking pairs is insufficient: $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,1)$ are pairwise nonparallel but the third is the sum of the first two. Independent vectors need not be perpendicular. To see the equivalence of the definitions, any nonzero coefficient in a zero combination would let you solve for its vector in terms of the others; independence rules that out.

topicCoverage.title: Linear Independence in Abstract Vector Spaces
Linear Span of Vectors in N-Dimensional Euclidean Space

correctAnswer.value:
A set is linearly dependent when at least one vector can be built as a linear combination of the others. That vector is redundant: removing it does not change the span. Equivalently, there are coefficients, not all zero, for which

$$c_1\vec v_1+\cdots+c_k\vec v_k=\vec0.$$

Geometrically, two nonzero vectors are dependent when they are parallel. Three vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ are dependent when they all lie in a plane through the origin, possibly in a smaller line or just at the origin. Any set containing the zero vector is dependent.

content.solution: Dependence does not require two vectors to coincide or be parallel. For example, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,1)$ are dependent because $(1,0)+(0,1)-(1,1)=(0,0)$; none of the three pairs is parallel. The phrase **not all zero** is essential: every set has the all-zero-coefficient combination. If $c_j\ne0$ in a zero combination, then $\vec v_j=-\sum_{i\ne j}(c_i/c_j)\vec v_i$, which expresses that vector using the others. Conversely, such an expression rearranges to a zero combination with a nonzero coefficient.
